2 Kings 1.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew Baalzebub as a god Israel's king should never have asked (Exodus 20:3), and they knew Elijah as the great prophet. They heard that the LORD answered a king who looked to another god.

culture.title: Baalzebub
culture.text: Baalzebub, lord of flies, was the god of Ekron. In the Gospels, Beelzebub is the name used for the prince of devils (Matthew 12:24).

culture.title: A hairy garment
culture.text: Elijah is recognized as an hairy man, and girt with a girdle of leather. John the Baptist dressed in camel's hair with a leather girdle (Matthew 3:4).

culture.title: Captains of fifty
culture.text: Armies were organized in units of fifties, hundreds, and thousands, each under a captain.

2 Kings 2.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew Elijah as the prophet who would come again before the day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5). They heard that Elisha received a double portion of his spirit, and that companies of prophets knew what the LORD would do.

culture.title: A double portion
culture.text: Elisha asks for "a double portion" of Elijah's spirit—the share of the firstborn son and heir (Deuteronomy 21:17).

culture.title: Salt in the spring
culture.text: Elisha heals Jericho's water by throwing salt into the spring. The spring at Jericho is still known as Elisha's Spring.

culture.title: Bald head
culture.text: Young men mock Elisha as "thou bald head." Bears come out of the woods and maul forty-two of them.

2 Kings 3.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew Moab as a longtime neighbor and rival. They heard how Elisha's word shaped the campaign.

culture.title: Tribute in wool
culture.text: Mesha was a sheep breeder who paid Israel 100,000 lambs and the wool of 100,000 rams—tribute paid in the land's chief product.

culture.title: Music and prophecy
culture.text: Elisha calls for a minstrel, and as the musician plays, the hand of the LORD comes upon him. Music accompanied prophecy in other places too (1 Samuel 10:5).

culture.title: Sacrifice on the wall
culture.text: Facing defeat, Mesha offers his eldest son as a burnt offering on the city wall. Child sacrifice in times of crisis is known among Israel's neighbors.

2 Kings 4.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew Elisha's ministry reached ordinary households. They heard accounts of the LORD's care through the prophet.

culture.title: Children sold for debt
culture.text: A creditor could take a debtor's children as bondservants. The widow is about to lose her two sons this way.

culture.title: A room on the roof
culture.text: The Shunammite woman builds a small walled chamber on the roof with a bed, table, stool, and lamp for Elisha—a common way of adding guest space.

culture.title: Wild gourds
culture.text: In famine, people gathered wild plants. Wild gourds can be bitter and poisonous, causing the cry "there is death in the pot."

2 Kings 5.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew that Jesus later pointed to Naaman's healing when he said many lepers in Israel were not healed (Luke 4:27). They heard that a foreign enemy commander found the God of Israel, while Elisha's own servant fell to greed.

culture.title: Rivers of Damascus
culture.text: Abana and Pharpar were rivers watering Damascus, making it a green oasis. To Naaman they seemed better than the muddy Jordan.

culture.title: Earth from Israel
culture.text: Naaman asks for two mules' loads of earth to take home, so he can worship the LORD on Israelite soil. Many believed a god was tied to his own land.

culture.title: Changes of raiment
culture.text: Naaman brings ten talents of silver, six thousand pieces of gold, and ten changes of clothing—fine garments were valued gifts.

2 Kings 6.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew the old warning that siege would bring terrible hunger (Deuteronomy 28:53). They heard that the LORD's army stood with Elisha even when no one could see it, and that mercy was shown to enemies.

culture.title: A borrowed axe-head
culture.text: Iron tools were valuable. The young man cries "Alas, master! for it was borrowed," because he could not easily replace it.

culture.title: Famine prices
culture.text: During the siege a donkey's head sold for eighty pieces of silver and a small measure of dove's dung for five. Sieges drove food prices to extremes.

2 Kings 7.audience: Lepers lived outside the city gate, as the law required (Leviticus 13:46). Readers would see four of them be the first to find the abandoned Syrian camp.

culture.title: A measure of fine flour for a shekel
culture.text: Elisha promises that prices will return to normal by the next day. Markets were held in the city gate.

culture.title: Hired armies
culture.text: The Syrians flee, thinking Israel has hired the kings of the Hittites and of the Egyptians against them. Kings often hired allied or mercenary forces.

2 Kings 8.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew Hazael as one of Israel's fiercest enemies (2 Kings 10:32). They heard that Elisha wept because he knew what Hazael would do, and that the Shunammite woman's land was restored by the king.

culture.title: Appealing for land
culture.text: The Shunammite woman left during famine and returns to find her land taken. She appeals directly to the king, who restores it.

culture.title: Forty camels of gifts
culture.text: Hazael brings "forty camels' burden" of goods from Damascus to consult Elisha—a lavish royal gift.

2 Kings 9.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew Elijah's words against Ahab's house (1 Kings 21:21–24). They heard how each word came true, and that the LORD's judgment came through a violent king, Jehu.

culture.title: Garments spread for a king
culture.text: The officers spread their garments under Jehu and blow a trumpet, proclaiming "Jehu is king." Crowds later spread garments before Jesus (Matthew 21:8).

culture.title: Driving furiously
culture.text: The watchman recognizes Jehu from a distance by the way he drives his chariot—"he driveth furiously."

culture.title: Painted eyes
culture.text: Jezebel paints her eyes with dark cosmetic and adorns her head before facing Jehu. Eye paint was common among women of rank.

2 Kings 10.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew Jehu ended Ahab's dynasty. They heard the warning against Baal worship in Israel.

culture.title: Heads in baskets
culture.text: The heads of Ahab's seventy sons are sent in baskets and piled in heaps at the gate of Jezreel. Assyrian reliefs show heaps of enemies' heads after conquest.

culture.title: Vestments for worship
culture.text: Jehu has robes brought out for all the worshippers of Baal, so they can be identified in the temple.

2 Kings 11.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew that Judah's kings were all descended from David, and that Athaliah was the only queen to rule in her own right. They heard that David's line survived through one hidden child.

culture.title: Guarding the king
culture.text: Jehoiada organizes the guards in shifts around the temple on the Sabbath, when the watch changed, to protect the boy king.

culture.title: Crowning and the testimony
culture.text: Joash is given the crown and "the testimony"—probably a copy of the covenant law—and anointed, as the people clap and shout "God save the king."

2 Kings 12.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew the temple as the center of worship, and they knew how often kings spent its treasures to buy peace. They heard that honest workmen and a simple collection chest got the repairs done.

culture.title: A chest with a hole in the lid
culture.text: Jehoiada sets a chest with a hole in its lid beside the altar, and the priests put in the money people brought. It is an early picture of a collection box.

culture.title: Paying tribute to stop an attack
culture.text: Joash sends the temple treasures to Hazael king of Syria, who withdraws from Jerusalem.

2 Kings 13.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew Elisha as the prophet who served Israel from the days of Ahab to Jehoash. They heard that even in his last hours, his word, and even his bones, carried the LORD's power.

culture.title: Arrows as a sign
culture.text: Elisha has the king shoot an arrow eastward and strike the ground with arrows. Acted signs gave prophetic words visible form.

culture.title: Burial in caves
culture.text: Elisha was buried in a tomb, likely a cave or rock-cut chamber. A dead man thrown into it revives on touching his bones.

2 Kings 14.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew Jonah son of Amittai as the prophet of the book of Jonah, and they knew Amos and Hosea spoke in Jeroboam II's days (Amos 1:1; Hosea 1:1). They heard that the LORD saved Israel through a king who did evil, because he saw their affliction.

culture.title: A fable of thistle and cedar
culture.text: Jehoash answers Amaziah's challenge with a fable: a thistle asking a cedar for its daughter, trampled by a wild beast. Fables were used to mock and warn.

culture.title: Breaking down the wall
culture.text: Jehoash breaks down four hundred cubits of Jerusalem's wall—a lasting humiliation for the city.

2 Kings 15.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew Assyria as the empire that would end the northern kingdom. They heard how quickly Israel's kings fell to plots, while Judah's kings did right but left the high places.

culture.title: Pul
culture.text: Pul is another name for Tiglathpileser III of Assyria. Menahem pays him a thousand talents of silver, raised by taxing wealthy men fifty shekels each.

culture.title: Deportation
culture.text: Assyria deported conquered peoples to other parts of its empire to break resistance. This is the first deportation of Israelites recorded in Kings.

2 Kings 16.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew Isaiah's words telling Ahaz to trust the LORD and not fear Syria and Israel (Isaiah 7:1–9). They heard that Ahaz chose Assyria instead, and changed the temple to please its king.

culture.title: Passing children through fire
culture.text: Ahaz makes his son pass through the fire "according to the abominations of the heathen." Israel's law forbade it (Deuteronomy 18:10).

culture.title: Copying an altar from Damascus
culture.text: Ahaz sees an altar in Damascus while meeting Tiglathpileser and has a copy built for the temple in Jerusalem.

2 Kings 17.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew the fall of the northern kingdom as a warning, and they knew the Samaritans of their own day as a people of mixed descent (2 Kings 17:24). They heard the writer blame Israel's long refusal to listen to the prophets.

culture.title: Resettlement
culture.text: Israelites are taken to Halah, Habor, and the cities of the Medes. Assyrian records of Sargon II claim the deportation of 27,290 people from Samaria.

culture.title: Gods of each nation
culture.text: Each settled people brought its own god—Succothbenoth, Nergal, Ashima, Nibhaz, Tartak, and others—while also fearing the LORD.

2 Kings 18.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew Hezekiah as a reforming king, and they knew Isaiah's part in this story (Isaiah 36–37). They heard a proud Assyrian officer ask what Hezekiah trusted in.

culture.title: Nehushtan
culture.text: Hezekiah breaks the bronze serpent Moses made (Numbers 21:9), because people were burning incense to it. It had been kept for centuries.

culture.title: Lachish
culture.text: Sennacherib besieged Lachish, a major city of Judah. Reliefs from his palace in Nineveh show the siege, and the siege ramp still survives at the site.

culture.title: Speaking in Hebrew
culture.text: Judah's officials ask Rabshakeh to speak in Aramaic (the Syrian language), the diplomatic language, rather than in Hebrew, which the people on the wall could understand.

2 Kings 19.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew Jerusalem was spared and that Sennacherib never took it. They heard Hezekiah take the threat to the LORD, and Isaiah answer.

culture.title: Spreading a letter before the LORD
culture.text: Hezekiah takes Sennacherib's threatening letter into the temple and spreads it before the LORD as he prays.

culture.title: Sennacherib's death
culture.text: Sennacherib is killed by his sons while worshipping in the temple of Nisroch. Babylonian records confirm he was murdered and succeeded by Esarhaddon.

2 Kings 20.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book lived in exile and knew Isaiah's warning about Babylon had come true (2 Kings 24:13). They heard that Hezekiah's prayer gave him fifteen more years, but that his pride in showing his treasure had a cost.

culture.title: A lump of figs
culture.text: A poultice of figs is placed on Hezekiah's boil. Figs were used as medicine in the ancient world.

culture.title: The shadow on the dial
culture.text: The shadow goes back ten steps on the stairway ("dial") of Ahaz. Steps or sundials were used to tell time by the sun's shadow.

culture.title: Hezekiah's tunnel
culture.text: Hezekiah made a pool and conduit to bring water into the city. The tunnel still exists under Jerusalem, with an ancient Hebrew inscription describing its digging.

2 Kings 21.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew Manasseh's reign as the reason the LORD gave for Judah's fall (2 Kings 24:3). They heard that even a good king's reforms could be undone by his son.

culture.title: Worship of the heavens
culture.text: Manasseh builds altars for "all the host of heaven" in the temple courts. Worship of sun, moon, and stars was central to Assyrian and Babylonian religion.

culture.title: Line and plummet
culture.text: Builders used a measuring line and a plumb line to check walls. God says he will stretch over Jerusalem the line of Samaria—measuring it for destruction.

2 Kings 22.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew Josiah as Judah's last great reforming king, and they knew the law's warnings (Deuteronomy 28). They heard a king answer God's word by tearing his clothes and humbling himself.

culture.title: Huldah the prophetess
culture.text: Josiah's officials consult Huldah, a prophetess living in Jerusalem's second quarter (the "college"), whose husband kept the royal wardrobe.

culture.title: Tearing clothes at the word
culture.text: When the book is read to him, Josiah tears his clothes—a sign of grief and repentance.

2 Kings 23.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew the word spoken long before at Bethel (1 Kings 13:2) and saw it fulfilled here. They heard that even the greatest reform could not turn aside the LORD's anger over Manasseh.

culture.title: Horses of the sun
culture.text: Kings of Judah had dedicated horses and chariots to the sun at the temple entrance. Josiah removes the horses and burns the chariots.

culture.title: Topheth
culture.text: Topheth in the valley of Hinnom was where children were burned in sacrifice to Molech. Josiah defiles it. The valley's name later gave rise to "Gehenna."

culture.title: Death at Megiddo
culture.text: Pharaoh Necho of Egypt marches north to the Euphrates to help Assyria against Babylon. Josiah goes against him and is killed at Megiddo.

2 Kings 24.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book lived in exile and knew Ezekiel and others were among the first captives (Ezekiel 1:2). They heard that the LORD sent Babylon according to the word of his prophets.

culture.title: Babylonian Chronicle
culture.text: A Babylonian clay tablet records that Nebuchadnezzar captured the city of Judah in his seventh year and appointed a king of his choice.

culture.title: Taking craftsmen
culture.text: Babylon deports the leaders, warriors, craftsmen, and smiths, leaving only "the poorest sort of the people of the land."

2 Kings 25.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book lived with these events and mourned them (Psalm 137; Lamentations 1). They heard that the book ends with a small sign of hope for David's line.

culture.title: Blinding a rebel king
culture.text: Zedekiah's sons are killed before his eyes, and then he is blinded and bound in bronze chains—punishment for breaking his oath to Babylon.

culture.title: Ration tablets
culture.text: Jehoiachin eats at the king of Babylon's table with a daily allowance. Babylonian tablets listing oil rations for Yaukin, king of the land of Yahud have been found.
